newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's Stoyanov short of majority -projection.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's Stoyanov short of majority -projection.

text.p: Bulgarians looked set to deliver a rebuff to their ex-communist rulers on Sunday by voting for a leading opposition figure as the country's next president.

According to an unofficial projection based on a random sample of polling stations, Petar Stoyanov of the Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) held a commanding lead over his main rival, Ivan Marazov of the Socialist party.
But the projection from the Bulgarian Association for Fair Elections and Civil Rights showed Stoyanov was still short of the absolute majority he needs to avoid a run-off next weekend.
The 44-year-old lawyer had won 43.1 percent of the vote against Marazov's 27.7 percent, according to the latest projection made by collating results from 160 of the country's 12,357 polling stations.
The projection placed George Ganchev of the Bulgarian Business Bloc third with 21.7 percent.
Other polling agencies produced similar results.
As polls closed, official estimates showed some 60 percent of the 6.75 million electorate in this former Soviet satellite had turned out to vote.
The Socialists have a secure majority in parliament -- where real power in Bulgaria lies -- but the UDF currently holds the more ceremonial post of president.

Political analysts had forecast, however, that a big rebuff for the Socialists this time would widen rifts within their ranks that have become more public since the still unsolved October 2 killing of former prime minister Andrei Lukanov.
Parliament is only half way through its four-year term but cabinet changes are a possibility.

The reform laggard of the ex-Warsaw Pact east European countries, this largely agricultural nation of just 8.4 million people has been slow to shake off its communist legacy and many older voters remember the old days fondly.

Pensioner Ana Georgieva, voting in central Sofia, recalled the free education her sons enjoyed under former dictator Todor Zhivkov and said her family could not afford to send her granddaughter to university.
"Everything went to ruins in 1989," Georgieva said.

Many of Bulgaria's two million pensioners are nostalgic for the greater security offered by one-party rule, when Zhivkov's state ensured food was cheap, even though freedom of speech and movement were restricted.
A feeling that Bulgaria's deepening economic woes are beyond resolution by politicians was especially marked in the countryside where turnout was generally lower.
"I don't see how a president -- whoever he is -- can change things," said Olga Netkova in the village of Negovan, 15 km (10 miles) northeast of Sofia.
While most other ex-Soviet states have seen some benefits from economic reform and are pressing for inclusion in NATO and the European Union, Bulgaria remains mired in its post-war legacy.

An ambitious privatisation programme remains largely stalled in the face of powerful vested interests while several foreign investors privately complain Sofia still looks more to Moscow for inspiration than Brussels.
Prices are rising, the unit of currency, the lev, is falling, interest rates are over 200 percent and foreign exchange reserves have plunged to about $505 million from $1.5 billion a year ago.
Said one member of an ethnic Turkish family in southern Bulgaria:"The politicians are not coming here. They have forgotten us -- even God has forgotten us." 271920 GMT oct 96
